newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuania's Landsbergis takes early election lead.
newsitem.headline: Lithuania's Landsbergis takes early election lead.

text.p: Lithuania's independence hero Vytautas Landsbergis looked set on Monday to avenge a bitter defeat four years ago by ex-Communists as early results from parliamentary elections put his Homeland Union party in front.

With 48 of the 2,037 electoral districts counted, the Homeland Union had 25.83 percent of the vote, the Christian Democrats 17.14 and the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP) of ex-Communists 13.06.
The only other parties above the five percent mark were the Social Democrats with 8.37 and the Centre Union 5.02.
Sunday's elections, the second Lithuania has held since it quit the former Soviet Union, were hit by voter apathy.
Turnout figures showed Lithuanians had failed to get excited about the elections. With two hours of voting to go, just over 50 percent of the electorate had turned out.
Landsbergis spearheaded the Baltic state's independence drive from Moscow in a struggle that helped bring down the whole Soviet empire.
But a shock reversal at elections in 1992 saw voters dump Landsbergis as the economy collapsed and his party was riven by in-fighting.
The Homeland Union has said it will work with the Christian Democrats, who stress traditional values in this Roman Catholic country.
Landsbergis was quick to blame voter apathy on four years of rule by the ex-Communists.
"It indicates disappointment with democratic institutions...It is the bad result of a bad job," he told Lithuanian television.

Sunday's vote was the first round of the elections, with a run-off set for November 10. The first round will decide 70 of the 141 parliamentary seats under a proportional system and the second round the rest under a majority vote.
Many Lithuanians say they have failed to notice big changes in their lives six years after the country left the former Soviet Union.
Opponents have accused the LDLP of corruption and cronyism and they also say it has reneged on promises of easing the pain of economic reforms.
Instead the party followed a path of austerity along International Monetary Fund guidelines.
The LDLP was badly hurt at the end of last year when a former prime minister withdrew his funds from a bank days before it was shut at the start of a banking crisis.
Foreign Minister Povilas Gylys, a leading LDLP figure, blamed the low turnout on general pessimism.
"Many of our former supporters are disillusioned because they do not see improvements in their social security," he said.
